*Tattvatrayanirṇayaḥ*, composed by Sadyojyotiḥ Śivācārya.

Having bowed to Śiva, by whose grace desired goals— both seen and unseen— are swiftly accomplished, I shall compose a commentary on the *Tattvatrayanirṇaya* (The Determination of the Three Principles), accompanied by the commentary composed by Aghoraśivācārya.

In this regard, first of all, the Teacher pays homage to the Supreme Lord alone, distinguishing Him by means of the subject matter to be expounded in the treatise he intends to compose, for the sake of its completion without obstacle:
"He bestows diverse fruits upon individual souls after having observed the variety of their bonds."
Arising without beginning through His own majesty and independent of anything else—homage, homage to Him! || 1 ||
"Anādyudayaḥ" means that whose arising is beginningless and whose manifestation consists of the cognitive and active powers regarding all objects due to its stainlessness;
the sense is that if one were to admit even such a being as having a beginning, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). For this very reason, He is not dependent on anyone;
the meaning is that He is independent (*svatantra*). Such is He who, by His own majesty in the form of *Śakti*, perceives the diversity of bondage.
To persons who are not independent due to being shrouded by impurity (*mala*), [the Lord] bestows diverse fruits.

Among them, to those whose impurities are matured, He grants the higher or lower liberation in accordance with the diversity of that maturation; to those whose impurities are not yet matured, He grants the fruit in the form of experience (*bhoga*) in accordance with the diversity of their karma, solely for the purpose of bringing about the ripening of those impurities.
By the statement "He gives," his quality of being the benefactor of all is established. And he is indeed Śiva;
salutations again and again to that Śiva, who is joined with that very Śiva-nature which is beginninglessly established as consisting of omniscience and omnipotence.

Having thus paid homage to his supreme teacher, he makes a formal declaration regarding the composition of this treatise: "Now, for the benefit of those of dull intellect, I shall briefly state a portion of the true meaning found in the Tantra, as it was learned from my teacher, to those who offer salutations. (2)

For here, the Teacher, having briefly illuminated the true nature of reality as established in the venerable *Raurava* through a compendium of principles (*tattvasaṃgraha*), now illuminates that which is established in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*. Therefore, at the conclusion of that [work], it is said: "Thus spoke Sadyojyotis, the author of the *Suvṛtti*, regarding the principles" (verse 57), because the *Suvṛtti* is established as being precisely the commentary on the venerable *Raurava*.

Regarding this, he will state in the conclusion: "This determination of the three principles has been briefly stated by the author of the commentary on the *Svāyambhuva* (verse 32). *Nati* means prostration. Śiva alone is the recipient of prostration (*natibhāk*) here, because he is performed by all beings; for, as the Lord of All, he alone is worthy of worship by everyone. In the *tantra*, that is, the scripture, of that Śiva—
"I shall speak for the benefit of those of dull intellect that which has been understood from the unbroken lineage of the Guru, handed down from the Supreme Lord.
Śambhu, Puruṣa, and Māyā—this triad of principles remains eternally pervasive and endowed with the power of agency; it stays awake even when the manifest world is in a state of sleep.

In this context, Śambhu is so called because he contemplates *śam*, which is bliss (*sukha*) characterized by the state of being unimpelled. By the word Śambhu, Śiva is denoted as inseparable from his inherent power (*śakti*). By the word *puruṣa*, used in the singular to denote the genus, all individual selves (*ātman*) are meant.
And by the word *māyā*, as uttered in the Tantras, both the pure and impure forms consisting of *māyā* and *mahāmāyā* are indicated.
The two material causes of the universe are stated [as follows]. As it is said in the venerable *Raurava*: "Above Māyā is Mahāmāyā" (4.28).
And that triad is eternal, because it is beginningless; for if they too had a beginning, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress, and because they are heard of as being eternal.
Furthermore, they are all-pervasive (*vibhu*). Among them, Śambhu and Puruṣa are indeed omnipresent; for if they were not omnipresent, they would be formless like space and so forth.

Because movement is impossible, it is not tenable that Śiva is the substratum of all things while the Self experiences the fruits of karma in another location; for Māyā pervades its own effects. And in this context, since impurity (mala) is by nature an eternal obscuration of the Self, its eternality and pervasiveness are established as a matter of course, and thus need not be stated separately.

Its appropriation [is as follows]: likewise, it is endowed with the power of agency (*kartṛśakti*). In that regard, both Pati and Puruṣa, because they are conscious, are endowed with the power of agency by virtue of being the creator of the world and the enjoyer; and precisely because of their agency, they are endowed with the power of cognition (*jñātṛśakti*). Furthermore, the very nature of consciousness consists of vision and action. As it is heard in the *Mṛgendratantravṛtti* (2.5): "Consciousness has the form of vision and action. And Māyā...
Presided over by the power of the Supreme Lord, the Creator, the triad of principles remains awake and indeed shines forth even when the category of effects has been subsumed. || 3 ||
Having thus stated their similarity, he states their difference:
"Śiva and Puruṣa are beyond enumeration, devoid of procreation, and endowed with consciousness;
Māyātattva, however, is one, joined with procreation, and devoid of consciousness. (4)
In this regard, the category of souls (*ātmavarga*) is exceedingly numerous due to its infinity;

Śiva as well, because he is the substratum of infinite conscious and unconscious entities and is thus endowed with an infinity of distinctions in a figurative sense, is exceedingly numerous by way of metaphor. Alternatively, [he is so called] because even among liberated souls, [Śiva is distinguished] by that which is manifested through the removal of impurities (*mala*).

Because of its union with Śiva-nature—which consists of the power of knowledge and action and encompasses all objects—it is designated by the term "Śiva," and thus its extreme plurality is stated. Furthermore, those two [Śiva and Śakti] are devoid of *prasava* (procreation), that is, transformation in the form of modification, due to their changelessness;
and as previously stated, they are endowed with consciousness. The *māyā*-tattva, however, whether pure or impure, is one, because it is the supreme material cause (*upādāna*).

For if there were multiplicity while lacking consciousness, then due to that multiplicity, it would necessarily be preceded by a cause. Furthermore, precisely because it is a material cause (*upādāna*), it must be endowed with the capacity to produce effects, and like clay and other such things, it would be insentient.

Having thus demonstrated the difference between Śiva and the souls (ātman) with respect to the principle of Māyā, he now says the following to show the difference between Śiva and the souls: "The Lords (Īśas) have their power (vīrya) set in motion; among them, one has the glory of qualities established from beginningless time."
From that [liberation], there is the stainlessness of the Lord of Liberation (Mukteśvara) regarding all objects, as well as [the perfection] of vision and action. || 5 ||

Those who possess active vigor (*pravṛttavīrya*) and the capacity for all objects are all indeed denoted by the term "Lord" (*īśa*) due to their autonomy. Among them, it has been stated that one is Paramaśiva, whose perfection of qualities is established from beginningless time. Consequently, the stainlessness (*vaimalya*) of the liberated souls (*muktātman*), who partake in equality with the Lord, and of the Lords such as the Vidyeśvaras, arises from that very Śiva acting as the instrumental cause.

And the manifestation of Śiva-nature has been accomplished. In that regard, the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) and others exercise their authority by the command of Śiva due to their connection with a portion of the impurity of office (*adhikāra-mala*); however, the liberated souls (*muktātman*) do not so engage, because they cannot be impelled by Him and because they fulfill the supreme grace [of others] through that very state. || 5 ||
But surely, even for Śiva, who is liberated from time immemorial, various distinctions such as *sakala* and *niṣkala*, as well as distinctions such as Īśāna and Tatpuruṣa, are heard in scripture;
therefore, he says:
"The group of [powers] was not previously created by him, since the Lord is established from time immemorial."
And that which is sung as the distinction between the complete and the incomplete is the domain of ritual action.

The group of effects (*kāryavarga*) consists of both pure and impure forms; it is preceded by *nati* (devotion) and preceded by the transformation of the appropriation of the pure and impure—the remainder being that "it arises. Therefore, within that [Principle] which is established as beginningless, there is the distinction of *sakala* and so forth, as well as the distinction of *sadyojāta* and so forth, which pertains to action—that is, the fivefold functions such as creation (*sṛṣṭi*).

Due to the distinction between His own activities, such as exertion (*udyoga*), and the distinctions in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the acts of creation and so forth, He is described in the scriptures by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), but not from an ultimate standpoint (*paramārthika*). As it is heard: "He is the possessor of authority (*adhikārī*), the enjoyer (*bhogī*), and the one who merges (*layī*), [all] by way of metaphorical designation"; and: "That distinction arises from the difference in functions (*kṛtyabheda*);
there is no distinction in the ultimate sense. Thus, Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta [are designated thus] due to the difference in their functions.

And as for the statement "it is divided": the distinction between the *sakala* (with parts) and *akala* (without parts) regarding the subject of the bound soul (*paśu*) is indeed real. To explain: the *sakala* is of two kinds. One is endowed with the three bonds (*bandha*) along with the connection to *kalā* and the other categories; the other remains for some time even after the exhaustion of karma through higher knowledge (*vijñāna*), etc., due to the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*). The *akala* is also of two kinds. Among these, one is joined with impurity (*mala*) and karma because *kalā* and the rest have been withdrawn by dissolution (*pralaya*).

The *pralayākala* is one who has dissolved [into the state of dissolution]. The *vijñānakevala* is one who, through the exhaustion of karma by means of knowledge (*vijñāna*), yoga, and so forth, is joined with only the residual impurity (*mala*).

The liberated one (*mukta*) is indeed free from all impurities. As it is said in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "Furthermore, the Self is known to exist in three states—the impure bound one, the one liberated by initiation, and the pure one; namely, the *kevala*, the *sakala*, and the *amala*. (6)
Now he describes the nature of the bound soul (paśu):
"The collection of qualities belonging to persons is like that of Śiva, yet it is entirely conjoined with something;
for by a single impurity (mala), it has been obstructed from time immemorial. (7)

The essential nature of all selves is also pervasive, consisting of consciousness and action, just like Śiva. And it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "Consciousness, whose form is vision and action, exists eternally in the self; for it is heard that in liberation it is 'all-facing' (omnipresent) in every respect" (*Viṣṇusaṃhitā* 2.5). And because that [consciousness] depends upon a manifestor, it belongs to all selves.

The essential nature [of the self] is understood to be obstructed by a certain single impurity (*mala*) produced since beginningless time. And that impurity, because it is beginningless, is indeed one.

For if it were manifold, then, being insentient like a jar or similar objects, another cause would have to be sought; consequently, an eternal obscuration of the selves would not be possible. Thus it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "Now, the beginningless impurity of persons... (33.1). || 7 ||
Therefore, being powerless, ignorant, and inactive without the manifestation of strength,
they are not able by themselves to manifest their own pure power, which extends to all objects.

Furthermore, because they are conjoined with impurity (*mala*), the selves (*ātman*) are dependent, ignorant, and inactive in the absence of the manifestation of their own power; therefore, the sense is that they require Śiva as the manifester of that [power]. Now, one might ask: "Will the selves effect the manifestation of their own power through knowledge and so forth? To show that this is incorrect, he says: "And they are not capable. The intention here is as follows: because impurity is a substance (*dravya*), it is like the eye...

Just as a cataract is not removed by mere knowledge, but rather by the action of an eye-physician, so too [ignorance] is not removed by mere knowledge, but only by the action of the Lord known as initiation (*dīkṣā*). This has been explained by us in detail in the *Tattvasaṃgrahalaghutīkā*. || 8 ||
Because their mastery over Śiva has not been achieved due to the obstruction by impurity (mala),
these [souls] must be restrained, bound, purified, and awakened by the Lord.

Because they are veiled by impurity (*mala*), their subjugation by the unobscured Śiva has not been performed; rather, it is established from beginningless time. For this reason, they are to be obstructed by the power of obstruction (*rodha-śakti*) and are to be bound by the fetters of *kalā* and so forth for the sake of experiencing the fruits of karma.

Here, "obstruction" refers to the concealment (*tirobhāva*) of the selves, consisting of the enjoyment of experiences according to their respective dispositions, brought about by the production of the efficacy of the bonds (*pāśa*).

And then, when the ripening of impurity has occurred, they are to be purified by initiation through the removal of the bonds such as impurity, and by that very manifestation of Śiva-nature, they become awakened. || 9 ||
Here, a further objection is raised: "Is it not better to postulate the presence of impurities and so forth within the powers of eternal knowledge and the rest?
True; however, that is not the case, because such a thing is not observed in the case of the Lord. (10)

[Objection: Surely, since the powers of knowledge and action are established as eternal, it is more appropriate to postulate impurity (*mala*) and so forth as their obscuring factors, and not otherwise; for how can such a thing be postulated when that [impurity] is observed to be occasional? To this, he says: "True.
Because that consciousness consisting of knowledge and action is seen to be of such an eternal nature in the Lord (*īśvara*), therefore it must also be so in the case of the Self (*ātman*).

Because that [Self] is of the nature of consciousness, its vision is never other than itself and is eternally so; otherwise, since the selves would be subject to modification, there would follow the defects of insentience, impermanence, and so forth—this is the intended meaning. || 10 ||
Furthermore, he states that in the absence of impurity (*mala*) and the rest, even the connection with a body and so forth is not possible for this [soul]:
"When there is a connection with the transformations of *māyā*, karma is joined; impurity (*mala*) is the cause for those subject to existence (*bhavin*).
The powers of impurity are distinct for each individual soul, and they obscure its qualities. (11)

Since the body and so forth are desired solely for the sake of experiencing the fruits of karma, and since such experience is impossible for the stainless liberated soul (*muktātman*), there is no connection with the body and other such factors. As it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "All states that arise from the existence of that [karma] belong to the bound soul (*paśu*) and are of the nature of *māyā*"; and likewise: "From karma come various bodies, as well as objects and instruments."

The reading there is: "of embodied beings" (*śarīriṇām*, *Svāyambhuva* 32.13). Now, if this is so, since impurity (*mala*) is unitary, would it not follow that when one is liberated, everyone would be liberated? To this he says: "the powers of impurity.

Because impurity possesses multiple powers fixed to each individual soul (*pratyātmaniyata*), upon the maturation and cessation of one [power], liberation belongs only to that [soul] which was obstructed by it, not to all.
The state of being. || 11 ||
He says this very thing:
"Impurity ceases from suppression, through the power of the person, by transformation over time;
due to the occurrence of a specific transformation, it [ceases] for someone at some time and in some manner. (12)
For impurity, undergoing transformation, ceases from its obscuration of the power of the Person (puṃśakti). And because it is insentient, it does not cease by itself;

rather, it is said to cease only through the activity of the Lord. Furthermore, that transformation—like that of lotuses whose nature is gradual unfolding—is not restricted to a specific time; thus he says: "a particular transformation" (pariṇativiśeṣa). || 12 ||

For this very reason, he states that due to the difference in the transformation [of the self], and because of the distinction between the means of realization corresponding to the degree of ripening of the impurities, there is a distinction between supreme and non-supreme liberation:
"Therefore, the various modes of arising for individuals are observed to result from their respective means of realization."
Thus, it occurs through time and through qualities; otherwise, it never occurs by the will of the Lord.
"This liberation is of seven kinds" (Yogabhikṣu 5.67), and so forth, as heard in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures;

this variety of emergence consisting of liberation, which arises from differences in the means (*sādhana*), differences in qualities such as devotion and faith, and differences in time, is possible only through specific transformations of impurity (*mala*), and not otherwise. Nor does this difference arise from God independently of that [impurity].
It does not exist, because that would entail the fault of partiality and other such defects; and for this [Lord], who bestows grace upon all, there is no partiality. || 13 ||
For this very reason, he states that the distinction between the *naiṣṭhikī* initiation and the others is also logically established:
"Thus, having observed the cause to be devoid of numerical limitation, it was declared by the Lord;
[this is] endowed with sound reasoning regarding liberation, and not otherwise, for there would be an infinity of means. (14)

The sense is that if the ripening of impurity were of a single uniform nature, then the means for its cessation and its result would likewise be of a single uniform nature. Furthermore, this classification of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the classification of the ripening of impurity and so forth have been explained by us in detail in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*.
In order to elaborate upon the very infinity of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), he says:
To whatever extent and by whichever fetters that impurity acts as an obstacle to one's spiritual welfare,
to that same extent it relinquishes its state of bondage when those [fetters] are removed.

Regarding the self, such as the *vijñānakala* and others, the impurity (*mala*) effects obstruction by means of as many fetters (*pāśas*) as it possesses. For the *vijñānakala*, the impurity acts as an obstructer through its own effects consisting of fetters, namely ignorance (*ajñatva*), inactivity (*akriyatva*), and susceptibility to affliction (*vyāghātabhāktva*). As it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "The flood of fetters [is said to be] 'by virtue of the power of that [impurity]' because of ignorance."

But for the *pralayākala*, [the Lord] effects obstruction through *karmas*; and for the *sakala* as well, He effects obstruction through those [karmas] which correspond to them, both in their common and uncommon forms, as well as through the worlds (*bhuvana*) and so forth associated with them. By means of those [entities] deposited together with the self, He causes him to abandon his state of bondage. || 15 ||
And therefore—
since such means for liberation from existence are seen in the scripture of Śiva, and they do not arise as logical in any other way. (16)

Since such means known as *dīkṣā*— which sever the bonds both individually and collectively, which are divided into the categories of *sakala* and so forth, which are distinguished by the divisions of *sādhara* and *nirādhāra*, and which are further differentiated by the types of *naiṣṭhikī* and so on—

are heard of in the scriptures, they are therefore logically consistent; otherwise, they would be untenable in the absence of a distinction among causes consisting of specific transformations of impurity (*mala*).

They do not exist. Therefore, a difference in the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), a difference in liberation (*mokṣa*) necessitated by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the scriptural injunctions, and a difference in the ripening of the impurity (*mala*) that is its cause must necessarily be admitted. Furthermore, the signs of the ripening of impurity are heard of in the scriptures: "For those embodied beings whose power descends so as not to turn back, the sign of that [descent] is an eagerness for liberation."

"Aversion toward worldly existence, devotion toward the devotees of Śiva, and faith in the ritual system taught by Him" (Mṛgendra-vṛtti 5.4–5), and so forth. Therefore, initiation must be performed by the gurus only after the ascertainment of these signs, and not otherwise.
In this regard, the question is: Who transforms the impurity in dependence upon karma alone from the variegated atoms;
and who, having extracted the variegation from the seed, bestows experience along with its means? (17)
The meaning is that because impurity (*mala*) is insentient, its own maturation is not logically possible. To this, he provides the answer: "only by depending on karma.

He who—conforming to the diversity of karma—extracts from the impure seed, the *māyā-tattva*, experience consisting of pleasure and pain, as well as its instruments such as the body and so forth, and produces them, is Śiva himself who, through his power of obstruction (*rodha-śakti*), also matures the impurity.
And in that regard, his agency within the impure path occurs solely through Ananta. As it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*:
"In the pure path, Śiva is said to be the agent; in the dark [impure] path, Ananta is the lord" (*Viṣamapada* 3.27). || 17 ||
Furthermore:
He who, during sleep, remains making the seed fit for production, and in whom the entire universe is deposited at the time of dissolution for the sake of rest; (18)

During the sleep [of dissolution], Śiva also renders Māyā, which possesses manifold powers, capable of further production; likewise, He ordains such beings as himself to be fit for experience once again. || 18 ||
Even while the universe is awake, it is karma that brings about the experience of beings;
yet the Lord, possessing great power, out of compassion always provides a means for its cessation. (19)
And it is the meaning that *karma* makes the actions of persons fit for experience (*bhoga*), that is, it ripens them. As it has been said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Even during [His] sleep, He remains awakening those fit for awakening, obstructing those to be obstructed, and ripening the *karma* of those possessing *karma*."
"Making the powers of *māyā* capable of manifestation, he perceives every category of object exactly as it is. (Vijñānabhairava 4.15)
Having projected the means of enjoyment and having established its causal basis,
it then seizes that [basis] along with the self and remains for the sake of rest.
"Because he is intent on the welfare of all beings for those who are subject to existence and weary of worldly life. And so it is said (Viṣṇupurāṇa 4.13–14).
Having thus demonstrated Śiva’s activity even during the dissolution (*pralaya*), he now describes his activity during the period of maintenance (*sthiti*): "While awake..."
Regarding the phrase "viśve 'pi" (even when all [are awake]): he who bestows great power—consisting of omniscience and omnipotence—upon the selves is the Lord (Īśāna).

Even while all are awake, because he is always endowed with compassion, he renders some karma, though accompanied by impurity (mala), fit for cessation through its ripening and experience. The meaning is that, for the sake of the ripening of impurity, he causes whatever karma has ripened to be experienced during the period of worldly maintenance (sthitikāla).
Furthermore:

Even prior to its cessation, for the sake of providing reinforcement to its power, that noose is seen to obstruct the strength of the person while receiving assistance from the power of the noose itself. (20)

Since even prior to the cessation of impurity, it is impossible for that insentient [matter] to undergo transformation (*pāka*) by itself, the Supreme Lord is seen to act—through the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*)—to obstruct the power of the *puruṣa* and provide assistance to the power of the *pāśas*, in order to strengthen its own capacity. Now, one might object: "But for the Lord who has set out to bestow grace upon the self, how can there be self-concealment?"

Is the favor [bestowed] through the fetters (pāśa) untenable? That is not so, because the impurity (mala) can indeed be removed through its very ripening (pāka). For the sake of that ripening, the Lord—through connection with the bondage of Māyā—inflicts the concealment (tirodhāna) consisting of the experience of worldly enjoyment, which brings about suffering, just as a physician applies caustic and the like; thus, even this is for the purpose of grace alone, and there is no contradiction. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "Just as..."

"Even though a physician causes pain with caustic substances and the like, he is not perceived as a cause of suffering for the patient, because he bestows a desired object upon him. (Vigrahavyāvartanī 7.18) || 20 ||
And therefore:
Having perceived that, one applies the instrument suitable for its cessation for the sake of human liberation;
this is held to be the transformation of the impurity (mala) through the loss of consciousness, like the ripening of a seed while dormant. (21)

Seeing that impurity (*mala*) has ripened and is ready for cessation, Śiva employs—meaning he applies—the instrument known as initiation (*dīkṣā*), which is the form of his own power, for the sake of liberating the bound soul (*paśu*). If this is so, since it is stated that the ripening of impurity is caused solely by the experience of karma, one might object that there would be no ripening of impurity during the dissolution (*pralaya*); to this, he says: "like a seed."

Since impurity (*mala*) is insentient, it was stated that its transformation (*pāka*) is indeed possible even at that time through the presiding influence of the sentient Śiva, as in the case of *māyā*. Here, the following objection is raised: "If Śambhu renders the impurity fit for cessation, then what [of it]?"
One who objects, saying that [the Lord] could not act simultaneously toward all selves, should be addressed as follows. || 22 ||
Having spoken thus, he says, "having questioned [the opponent] in this manner," namely: "Thus objecting":
"Why does one not perform all that is to be experienced (*bhogya*) through one's own karma simultaneously, or why not on that very day? [The opponent replies:
'There is no contradiction because of plurality; the power of being experienced at another time is stronger. (23)
"Or on that very day" means: at the very moment they have arrived.

Now, if it is argued that because actions such as the Aśvamedha sacrifice and the killing of a Brahmin have contradictory fruits, their enjoyment cannot possibly occur at one and the same time, he says—refuting this—that "this is not a valid resolution. || 23 ||
To explain why it is not [always] in a state of meditative absorption (samādhi), he says:

"Because power capable of producing all transformations is always present in the Lord, in the seed, and in that which is subject to becoming; hence there is both omnipotence and the state of being an enjoyer. (24)
Therefore, the Lord, having created numerous groups for the performance of tasks and so forth,
simultaneously causes the Person to enjoy all fruits through the seed.
Since Śiva possesses the power capable of producing both common and uncommon transformations of Māyā,

and since within Māyā there exists the pervasiveness of all karmic fruits, as well as the pervasiveness and the state of being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) in the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*), therefore Śiva, having simultaneously produced many bodies and so forth from the principle of Māyā (*māyātattva*), [assigns] all karmas to the person (*puruṣa*).
The consequence that "one should feed [the self]" would also follow for your position. || 24–25 ||

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) raises an objection once more: "But surely we infer that Śambhu causes those very actions to ripen, having observed them being experienced in succession; thus, the principle is the same in both cases. (26)

From the observation that objects of experience occur sequentially, it is inferred that the ripening of karma is likewise sequential; Śiva brings this about, in accordance with the fitness for ripening, just as the sun causes the blooming of lotuses and other flowers. Therefore, for us, there is no contingency of experiencing all karmas simultaneously. If this is so, then for us as well, the signs of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*)—such as detachment from worldly existence and devotion to Śiva—occur only sequentially within the self.

Having observed [the descent of grace], one infers that such a ripening of impurity (*malapāka*) is the cause of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). Therefore, since the ripening of impurity does not occur for all simultaneously, we too are certainly not to be held accountable. As it has been said: "Where there would be a fault for both sides... (See *Laukikanyāyasāhasrī*, maxim no. 139; see commentary on the *Mālinīvijayottara-tantra* (*Ma0 pā0 vṛtti*), *Vidyāpāda*, pp. 218–219, note 22).
Alternatively, the rebuttal is equal: "One should not be the sole object of questioning when there is such a determination of meaning. With this intention, he says:
"It is the same" (samānam). || 26 ||
He elaborates on this very point:
"Having understood that the task has been declared, the cessation of impurity is attained here;
for even Maheśvara is capable of effecting such fitness. (27)

For here, having observed that the effect described—consisting of the performance of initiation—is inseparable from the descent of power (śaktipāta), the cessation of impurity (mala) is known; therefore, by observing that the effects occur sequentially, it is inferred that Śiva brings about the ripening of impurity only gradually and not instantaneously—this is the meaning. || 27 ||

Since the ripening of impurity (*mala*) and so forth is observed to occur only gradually during the period of their persistence, even at the time of dissolution (*saṃhāra*), the ripening of impurity and the rest must likewise conform to the capacity of those to be ripened; it is not the case that the ripening of all occurs simultaneously. Therefore, even when questioned regarding this matter, you must provide an answer.
Therefore, with the intention that your simultaneous inquiry regarding the impurity and its digestion is not appropriate toward us, he says:

"And thus, since the womb is fit [for conception] during sleep, you, being questioned regarding the [digestion of] karma, must provide an answer concerning the period of duration which is simultaneous [with that state]. (28)

The fitness of the womb (*yoni*) consists in the production of the capacity for birth; however, the fitness of *karman* for the yielding of its fruit is simply its ripening (*pāka*). The remainder is easy to understand. || 28 ||
To explain how the subsequent subject matter is to be understood, he says:
"Just as, at the beginning of creation, when there is no fixed rule, whatever object comes into being for however long a time, so indeed does it come to be by the Lord. (29)
"It can be done"— this [statement] is the same regarding liberation and its cause.
Thus, when the creation, maintenance, or dissolution of the body and so forth is observed as being devoid of any fixed rule for their arising,
whatever object arises from within the streams of illusion (māyāsrotas) at whatever time and in whatever manner, that very object [remains] for that duration.

The answer to your question regarding the simultaneity of the production of the effects of *māyā* must be stated as follows: such [simultaneity] can be brought about by the Lord (*Īśvara*) at the proper time, and not otherwise. It has been stated that the same applies to the ripening of karma and so forth.

Furthermore, this same solution applies to the question regarding the simultaneity of the granting of liberation, or to the question regarding the simultaneity of the ripening of the impurity (*mala*) which is its cause.
Thus he says: "This is equal. (29)

And since the substantial nature of this impurity, as well as its oneness and so forth, have been explained in detail in the scriptures, he says: "Enough with the complete description of the true nature of impurity. (30)

In the scriptures, [the objection that] oneness and so forth would be sublated in the absence of an infinity of powers is refuted by the reasoning arising from the teaching [of the scriptures], which is headed by the infinity of powers. (31)

As it is heard [in scripture]: "That which is one, belonging to all beings, beginningless, dense, and great, abiding within each individual soul, and possessing a multitude of powers that perish at the end of its own time" (Mṛgendra-vṛtti 7.8), and so forth—that is its nature;
and as previously stated, its infinity of powers cannot be excluded from the *puruṣas* except upon the liberation of a single one.
Because it would follow that everyone is liberated, or else it would follow that not even a single person could be liberated, he says: "the infinity of powers.
And since this essential nature of impurity—consisting of infinite power and so forth—is established by scripture and by reasoning, he says:

"headed by the infinity of powers. The word "indicated" (*uddiṣṭam*) is to be connected with what precedes. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [terms such as] beginninglessness and the rest are included.
It is grasped [as follows]: "That which is heard—whether it be beginningless or recent—is the cause of that; otherwise, it would obstruct even those who are liberated;

therefore, effort toward liberation would be in vain" (*Mṛgendravidyāpāda-vṛtti*, 7.9), and so forth. Furthermore, this investigation into impurity (*mala*) has been demonstrated by us in detail in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*; thus, it should be understood from that very source.
However, it is not written here for fear of excessive prolixity. || 30-31 ||
Now, the conclusion of the section:

This determination of the three principles has been stated in brief by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*), with the intention of removing from persons their beginningless state of insentience (*jaḍatā*) regarding the *Svāyambhuva* [Tantra]. (32)
Because their knowledge and action are veiled by beginningless impurity (*anādimala*), the insentience (*jaḍatā*) propounded by the Naiyāyikas and others is removed from the selves.
Since they are immutable, that which obscures them is *mala*; that which exists as long as it [mala] exists is *māyā*; and Śiva, who effects its cessation, is briefly expounded here. || 32 ||
By the preceptor named Śrīmad-ghoraśiva, who is renowned in the world for his commentary on the *Śrījanyā*, who adorns the *Kuṇḍina* lineage among the Colas,
and who is pure through his worship of the dust of the lotus feet of Śrī-Sarvātmaśiva.
This brief commentary on the *Śrītattvatrayanirṇaya* has been composed.
Thus ends the *Tattvatrayanirṇayavṛtti* composed by the teacher Aghoraśiva.
